gist: Daniel, a University of Toronto mathematics professor working in algebraic geometry, gives a practitioner's audit of frontier-model math results: the models are now genuinely strong at applying known techniques and grinding long computations, but stall on theory-building and on conjectures believed true, and verification — not generation — is the binding constraint on longer proofs. He argues the more consequential risk is institutional: AI-generated 'slot machine' papers are flooding arXiv, models appear mode-collapsed onto similar reasoning paths, and the incentive structures that build human mathematical capital have not adapted.

insights.claim: The strongest fully autonomous AI mathematics result to date, per a working algebraic geometer, is the mid-May solution to the unit distance problem, notable because the community believed the statement was true and the model produced a counterexample by importing classical 1960s techniques from an unrelated area into the study of point configurations in the plane.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: The bar for a genuinely 'creative' AI math result is technique transfer across fields plus an unexpected answer — a concrete rubric for discounting the majority of lab announcements that merely apply in-domain methods.
insights.quote: my favorite uh like fully autonomous result by an AI so far is the solution to the Irish unit distance problem which I think was announced in midMay

insights.claim: The proposed test for whether an AI-produced theorem matters is post-hoc fruitfulness — whether other mathematicians reuse its ideas — and the unit distance result passed, with its techniques then used to refute other open questions including the sum-product conjecture over the real numbers.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Gives a lagging but falsifiable metric for AI-for-science claims: track downstream citation and technique reuse rather than announcement volume.
insights.quote: a bunch of mathematicians took those ideas and used them to find counter examples to a bunch of other interesting open questions so for example like the sum product conjecture over the real numbers

insights.claim: Frontier-model math announcements span a spectrum from fully autonomous to semi-autonomous to results where the AI contribution is not disclosed at all, and a common pattern is 'last mile' work where human mathematicians did the deep prior work and the model took the final step.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Headline 'AI solved X' claims should be discounted by autonomy level; most published wins are last-mile completions, not independent discovery.
insights.quote: some kind of results I would characterize as like last mile like where some recent work was done like quite deep work done by a group of human mathematicians and then the AI kind of took the final step

insights.claim: The rank 30 elliptic curve construction produced by Claude Fable with Levent Poge and collaborators cannot be assessed because no methods have been released, and historically such record-setting constructions are 'cool' but land on a website of records rather than in a top journal.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: A widely circulated Anthropic math win is, in expert terms, an incremental record extension over the prior rank 29 example — useful for calibrating how much a viral lab result actually moves the field.
insights.quote: the typical place a result like this might go is like someone's website of records

insights.claim: A model-generated mathematical result cannot be evaluated at the moment of announcement — only in retrospect — because problems thought to need deep new ideas sometimes don't, and vice versa, which is equally true of human mathematics.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Structurally, AI-for-science progress cannot be scored on the announcement news cycle, which is exactly when capital and narrative react to it.
insights.quote: one thing I always say about a model result is like you cannot evaluate it except in retrospect

insights.claim: Disclosure norms around AI math wins are informal and lag the announcements — the researchers behind the recent Claude results tweet outcomes first and release traces or PDF writeups slowly, so the community often cannot tell how much autonomy or scaffolding was involved.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: An evaluation vacuum sits between claim and verification, which is where hype premia form; watch for whether labs standardize method disclosure.
insights.quote: a lot of these nice recent results have have come from Levent with unclear amounts of autonomy

themes.theme: Where frontier models are strong and where they stall

insights.claim: Frontier-model mathematical output reads as recognizably human rather than alien — the released chain of thought resembles a mathematician's own reasoning and contains no 'move 37' moment — so the gains look like compressed human technique, not a new form of cognition.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'alien superintelligence discovers new math' narrative; the near-term value is scaled expert labor, which is priced very differently.
insights.quote: It's not like there's some you know move 37 or whatever. Um it's like a human mathematician doing math.

insights.claim: Models' comparative advantage in research mathematics is grinding out long technical computations and pulling together technical ideas from many areas and papers a given human would not have read — a profile that maps to a real and well-rewarded style of human mathematical career.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: The displaced work is technique-application and literature-synthesis labor, which is where most working researchers actually sit — not the small tail doing conceptual innovation.
insights.quote: there'll be things that rely on the model strengths like their ability to like grind out along computation or like you know pull together kind of technical ideas for many areas

insights.claim: Models remain weak at the non-rigorous core of research mathematics — carrying a vague philosophy or analogy between two objects and making it precise — and so far cover only a narrow band of what mathematicians actually do.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Defines the remaining human moat concretely: problem formulation and analogy-building, not proof execution.
insights.quote: they seem like weaker in things like intuition or like having some big picture point of view

insights.claim: Models cannot do theory building autonomously but can already do something interesting on it when hinted, and the working heuristic offered is that a capability achievable today with roughly a hundred bits of hints becomes unhinted in about six months.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: A cheap leading indicator for capability forecasting: measure how much human hinting a task still requires, and extrapolate the hint budget to zero.
insights.quote: if they can do it with like a hundred bits of hints or whatever in six months, maybe they can do it without hints

insights.claim: Models are strong on conjectures that turn out to be false because refutation only requires exhibiting a specific construction, and weak on conjectures embedded in a large theoretical framework where the evidence points to truth and genuinely new machinery is required.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: The single most predictive filter for which mathematical results fall next to AI: counterexample-shaped problems, not framework-completing ones.
insights.quote: these conjectures fit into some very broad theoretical framework which means that like we actually have a lot of evidence that they're true

insights.claim: The guest explicitly disclaims capability skepticism, expects the upward trajectory to continue into theory building, and attributes the current gap to a missing training setup rather than a fundamental limit — the hard part being how to reward intermediate progress on a fuzzy skill.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: An informed insider treats conceptual mathematics as an RL environment design problem, implying the gap closes on lab engineering timelines rather than research-breakthrough timelines.
insights.quote: I'm not a skeptic of continued capabilities growth.

themes.theme: Reading lab strategy: natural-language RL vs. formal proof

insights.claim: Because the labs are scaling informal natural-language reasoning rather than training on Lean-verified proofs, the guest infers the underlying techniques will generalize well to domains that are not cheaply verifiable — cutting against the standard 'math is progressing because it is a verifiable domain' explanation.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: If correct, math capability gains are a leading indicator for non-verifiable knowledge work generally, rather than a special case that stays contained.
insights.quote: my sense is that because they're you know primarily scaling in formal reasoning like probably the techniques are going to generalize to other domains pretty well

insights.claim: Anthropic and OpenAI models are at rough capability parity in research mathematics, solving a very similar collection of problems, with announcements typically leapfrogging each other within days.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: No durable model-level differentiation in the highest-prestige reasoning benchmark, which weakens per-lab moat arguments built on math headlines.
insights.quote: it actually seems like they're they're solving a very similar collection of problems

insights.claim: Anthropic's models were not useful for research mathematics for a long stretch and only caught up to ChatGPT around Opus 4.5 or 4.6, which is why this practitioner's habit and usage still defaults to OpenAI's models.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Illustrates habit lock-in among expert users: capability parity does not immediately reverse usage share once a competitor established the workflow first.
insights.quote: for a long time um the claw model models were just like not useful for research math and then I think maybe around opus 4.5 or opus 4.6 they like more or less caught up

insights.claim: In expert use, OpenAI's 5.6 gives clearer exposition and a more accurate model of what the reader already knows, while Claude oscillates between explaining trivialities and skipping steps — though both are judged poor at theory of mind.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Differentiation among frontier models at expert level is showing up in explanation quality and audience modeling, not raw problem-solving — a product surface worth watching.
insights.quote: 5.6 is giving a more accurate theory of mind of what it assumes I know and don't know

insights.claim: Published mathematics is a poor proxy for how mathematicians actually reason — papers and textbooks are polished and strip out motivation, which is why understanding a research direction usually requires talking to the researcher — implying a structural gap in the available training corpus for mathematical intuition.
insights.speaker: host (a16z)
insights.so_what: Identifies tacit reasoning traces as the scarce data asset for the next capability step, a plausible target for lab data acquisition and expert-annotation businesses.
insights.quote: most of the papers are crisp and like polished. The textbooks certainly are just show very little motivation of how something is developed

themes.theme: Verification, not generation, is the binding constraint

insights.claim: The fact that models produce short clever proofs is a symptom of a capability ceiling rather than aesthetic virtue — short proofs are what can currently be checked, and on long arguments the models may not know they are wrong.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Reframes a talking point labs use as evidence of elegance into evidence of a verification bottleneck — the actual gate on longer-horizon reasoning products.
insights.quote: the uh reason they're not producing long complicated proofs is that they cannot

insights.claim: OpenAI's recently released list of 10 solved problems were all formalized in Lean, which is strong evidence they are true, and the guest infers the labs internally hold many more solutions they could not formalize or check — either because prerequisites are missing from the library or because the proofs are too long.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Published lab results are selected on verifiability, so external benchmarks systematically understate raw capability while overstating reliable capability.
insights.quote: with these this recent list of 10 problems uh released by OpenAI, those were all formalized in lean

insights.claim: An 800-page AI-generated claimed proof of resolution of singularities in positive characteristic was recently posted publicly and is, on calibration, almost certainly wrong — no human has read it and current models cannot check work of that length.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: A concrete example of unverifiable AI output entering the scientific record, which is the failure mode that erodes trust in the corpus itself.
insights.quote: someone recently posted a claimed proof of resolution of singularities and positive characteristic which was 800 AI generated pages

insights.claim: Scaffolding built to elicit long proofs actively degrades reliability, because pushing a model out of its rigorous mode to be creative is the same move that makes it stop refusing to assert wrong things.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: A direct reliability-vs-output-length tradeoff in agent harness design; length of generated artifact is a negative quality signal, not a positive one.
insights.quote: any harness that can elicit a 250 page paper is probably not being very careful about what it's producing

insights.claim: Models cannot yet do the fuzzy structural check that humans use on long proofs — stress-testing whether an argument would prove something known to be false — as shown by a paper experts immediately recognized as broken from its structure, which the models still fail to flag or diagnose.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: This is a specific, currently-unsolved eval that maps directly onto the same weakness in coding agents — good at local syntax, weak at global architecture.
insights.quote: they're also not able to do this kind of overall uh kind of big picture tax checking which is kind of like how people in practice check papers

insights.claim: Models will still emit proofs they themselves can identify as wrong when asked a follow-up question, though reliability has improved markedly over the past six months.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Self-critique capacity outruns first-pass output quality, which is a cheap product-level fix (mandatory self-check passes) available before any model upgrade.
insights.quote: they will still sometimes produce things that are just wrong and they know they're wrong

themes.theme: Slop economics and the collapse of publication incentives

insights.claim: Academic mathematics currently rewards a slot-machine strategy: a job-seeking postdoc can generate papers proving old conjectures at volume, and the guest ran the experiment with Codex — asking it to find five recent algebraic geometry conjectures and prove them — producing three bad but correct papers in about an hour.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Publication as a credential is being commoditized within an hour of compute, which forces a repricing of academic output metrics across the sciences.
insights.quote: go online, find five recent conjectures in algebraic geometry and prove them... I've run this experiment and with some back and forth, I was able to, you know, in an hour get like three, you know, quite bad papers

insights.claim: Multiple groups are independently posting three to five papers containing the exact same proof of the exact same theorem within days of each other, which is direct field evidence that frontier models are mode-collapsed onto identical reasoning paths.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Observable mode collapse in the wild caps the aggregate research value of throwing more inference at open problems — a thousand users converge on one answer rather than a thousand answers.
insights.quote: three or four or five papers with the exact same proof of the exact same theorem have come out in within a couple days of each other, which is clearly, you know, some situation where someone's playing the slot machine

insights.claim: Preprint volume in mathematics has risen sharply and most of the new material is low quality, with much of the slop coming from credentialed professionals responding to publication incentives rather than from amateurs.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: The incentive failure is inside the institution, so gatekeeping amateurs will not fix it — the repair has to come from changing what professional output is rewarded.
insights.quote: there's, you know, been a huge uptick in post to archive, mostly not very interesting

insights.claim: The influx of non-expert AI-assisted math activity is judged net positive despite the search costs it imposes, because broad enthusiasm for mathematics is itself valuable — a deliberately contrarian read against the prevailing 'AI slop' complaint.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Distinguishes two things usually conflated in the slop debate — noise from newcomers versus gaming by insiders — and only the second is treated as damaging.
insights.quote: to me it seems like just the fact that there's lots of people excited about math is like kind of a positive

insights.claim: The general pattern is a classic technology-diffusion dynamic: a tool that does something slightly worse but far cheaper floods the market with low-quality output that displaces prior high-quality output, and capturing quality gains instead requires deliberate redesign of institutional incentives.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: A transferable model for any AI-exposed knowledge industry: expect a quality trough first, and price the institutions that successfully redesign incentives as the winners.
insights.quote: you have a new technology that's doing something a little bit worse than was previously done but much cheaper and so you get a lot of suddenly a lot of like lowquality outputs that are displacing previous high quality outputs

themes.theme: Human capital as the scarce input

insights.claim: Frontier mathematics rests on a pipeline of thousands to millions of people learning to think mathematically, so a small elite cannot be sustained independently of the mass base — meaning any AI-driven collapse in incentives to train degrades the frontier with a long lag.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Applies to any expertise-dependent industry adopting AI: the visible productivity gain arrives years before the invisible pipeline damage shows up.
insights.quote: you need a an entire mathematical community to support a small group of people who are on the frontier like you just without the pipeline then the pipeline doesn't exist

insights.claim: Even under the assumption that models become robustly superhuman, the argument for keeping humans engaged is that the optimal allocation is not what actually gets chosen — handing research direction to models gives no guarantee they pursue broad fundamental work rather than the direct instrumental path.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Separates the capability question from the direction-setting question — a superhuman model does not automatically produce a well-diversified research portfolio.
insights.quote: there's no reason to think that you know if we hand over control of whatever math research to the models and just let them do their own thing that it will do the optimal thing

insights.claim: Progress in mathematics historically comes from many people pursuing idiosyncratic personal curiosity so the frontier expands uniformly and opportunistic connections appear, which is precisely what subordinating exploration to models threatens — yielding one mathematician duplicated a thousand times instead of a million different ones.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Diversity of search, not throughput of search, is the scarce input in discovery — an argument that more inference compute has sharply diminishing returns without diverse human direction.
insights.quote: if what you're getting is like one mathematician duplicated a thousand times or like actually you know a million different mathematicians doing a million different things

insights.claim: The stated purpose of mathematics is producing understanding rather than papers, and understanding that resides only in model weights is characterized as deeply unsatisfying — which is why the guest treats incentive redesign, not capability, as the field's central problem.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Defines the acceptance criterion expert communities will apply to AI-generated science: legibility and transferred understanding, not just correct artifacts.
insights.quote: the goal of mathematics is not to produce mathematics papers um like it's to produce some kind of understanding uh so maybe okay maybe that some of that understanding resides in model weights or something to me that's like pretty unsatisfying

insights.claim: Instructors are reporting a bimodal outcome distribution in classes — one group figuring out how to leverage the new tools and another outsourcing homework and then failing everything else — and institutions are not adapting fast enough to the split.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: A measurable early signal of AI-driven skill divergence in the labor pipeline, and a market for tooling and assessment that forces the productive mode.
insights.quote: people start talking about a biodal distribution in their classes where there's some people who are really like figuring out how to take advantage of new tools and other people who are just like letting them do their homework and then bombing everything else

insights.claim: Mathematics is not unusually exposed to AI, only unusually public about it — the guest's view is that most computer-based professions are already seeing a large share of work done by models without a comparable public reckoning, and math gets the spotlight because math capability is useful marketing for the labs.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Treat the visible disruption of academic mathematics as a leading, publicly observable proxy for quieter displacement across other computer-mediated professions.
insights.quote: anything you do at a computer like probably a huge amount is being done by the models at this point and then like there not having a public reckoning about it

themes.theme: How a working mathematician's practice actually changed

insights.claim: On long-running research projects that predate AI, the models are described as not that useful and primarily a substitute for Google — the real change is that they unlocked an entirely new set of coding-dependent projects the guest would otherwise have procrastinated on for six months.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Expert AI adoption shows up as new activities added rather than acceleration of existing deep work — an adoption pattern that inflates usage metrics without moving core productivity.
insights.quote: it's primarily kind of a substitute for Google or something like I might use it to like learn about some related topic

insights.claim: The concretely valuable research workflow is massively parallel example generation — dispatching roughly ten subagents at a time to work through hundreds or a thousand examples in search of a phenomenon — which mirrors the historically productive experimental style behind big-data conjectures like Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Points at where inference spend actually converts to research value today — parallel empirical search, not single-shot proof generation.
insights.quote: if you want to find an example of something, you can just ask it to find, you know, work through a thousand examples in parallel or maybe 10 examples at a time

insights.claim: In the guest's one published paper with real model contribution, Gemini deep think proved lemmas only after he hand-worked examples and found a better statement — and his own refusal to grind out the brutal calculation is what produced the superior conceptual result, whereas a model would have emitted ten pages of calculation with no insight.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Human cognitive limits function as a discovery mechanism, so removing the grinding constraint can yield correct results while destroying the understanding they would have generated.
insights.quote: it will output like the worst proof you've ever seen, like 10 pages of like just brutal calculation with no insight whatsoever

insights.claim: Despite building his own harness in Codex, the guest deliberately avoids autonomous mathematics and uses models mainly to help him understand things — an explicit choice to stay in the loop rather than optimize for output volume.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: Expert users are self-selecting into comprehension-preserving workflows over automation, which is a product design signal for tools aimed at high-end knowledge workers.
insights.quote: I personally I do not enjoy uh autonomous mathematics very much so I mostly mostly do not use the harness I mostly try to use it to help me understand stuff

insights.claim: The guest rejects aesthetic beauty as a research selection criterion in favor of doing 'physics except with concepts' and asking what will open up further understanding, and identifies abandoning a proof because it feels ugly as a common failure mode among young mathematicians.
insights.speaker: Daniel (guest, mathematics professor, University of Toronto)
insights.so_what: A selection heuristic — fundamentality and downstream leverage over elegance — that transfers directly to choosing which research or technical bets to fund.
insights.quote: I like to think of what I'm doing like doing kind of physics except with concepts
